sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Fayette County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
A Fayette County bill touches three public offices. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values each parcel, the Sheriff collects the current year's payment, and the County Clerk picks up bills that run late. Because Lexington and Fayette County merged their governments on January 1, 1974, the sheriff states there is no separate city bill: one statement covers every taxing district.

The PVA works from 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, in Lexington (phone 859-246-2722, fax 859-246-2729) and says in plain terms that it neither sets tax rates nor takes payments. The sheriff's Property Tax Division is in Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse at 150 North Limestone, reachable at 859-252-1771. Its counter is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays and stays open until 6:00 p.m. through October. The sheriff reports collecting over 110,000 bills worth nearly $260 million a year.

The bill pays for the Commonwealth, Fayette County Public Schools, the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (LFUCG), the county extension and soil conservation districts, the health department, Lextran and a park fund. Property in the Downtown Lexington Management District carries a further charge.

sections.h2: How is a Fayette County property tax bill calculated?
sections.html:
The bill equals the assessed value, minus any exemption, times the rate for the property's tax district, per $100 of value. Every parcel is valued as of January 1 at what the PVA calls fair cash value: the most probable price in an open sale between a willing buyer and a willing seller.

Rates depend on which city services a parcel receives. The seven residential districts on the PVA's chart share the same state, school, general services, extension, conservation, health, Lextran and park fund lines, and differ only in refuse, street light, street cleaning or full-service charges.

Real property rates in Fayette County for 2026, in dollars per $100 of assessed value, by tax district
DistrictServices billed on top of the base rateTotal rate
1Full services1.2598
2General services only1.0868
3Refuse1.2238
4Street lights1.1138
5Refuse and street lights1.2508
6Street lights and street cleaning1.1228
7Refuse and street cleaning1.2328

As an illustration only, a home assessed at $293,500 (the Census median value for owner-occupied homes in the county) in District 1 would owe about $3,698, since 2,935 hundreds times 1.2598 is roughly that figure. The same value in District 2 comes to about $3,190. Properties certified as abandoned and blighted by the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission pay an extra $1 per $100, and Downtown Lexington Management District parcels pay an extra $0.10 per $100.

sections.h2: When are Fayette County property tax bills due?
sections.html:
Payment is due by the end of December, and early payers get a discount. For 2026, statements were mailed in the last week of September and were due in mailboxes by October 1. Anyone still without a bill by about October 10 can call 859-252-1771 for a duplicate, because an unreceived bill does not excuse payment.

  • October 1 to November 1: pay the face amount less 2 percent.
  • November 2 to December 31: pay the face amount. The sheriff's online portal warns that payments after December 31, 2026 draw a late fee.
  • January 1 to January 31: 5 percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 10 percent penalty with a further 10 percent add-on.
  • After April 15: the bill is delinquent at 21 percent and moves to the County Clerk.

Payment options include the sheriff's counter (cash, check or money order), any Lexington Republic Bank lobby through January 31 with the bill coupon, the online portal (card or bank debit, with a convenience fee the sheriff does not receive) and mail to PO Box 34148, Lexington, KY 40588-4148. A mailed payment counts at the amount due on its postmark date, and a postage meter stamp is not accepted as proof. The sheriff cannot take installments or grant extensions, and a returned check adds a $35 fee.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Fayette County assessment?
sections.html:
Speak with a PVA assessor first, and only then file an appeal with the County Clerk. The PVA reviews each of its roughly 300 assessment areas every three to four years under a state quadrennial plan, and neighborhood sales drive most reassessments. Many owners receive a notice in April that includes a map of recent sales close to the property.

In 2026 the PVA wanted conferences finished by Monday, May 18, and the clerk had to receive the appeal to the Local Board of Tax Appeals by Wednesday, May 20. Kentucky's statewide calendar places the tax roll inspection in the 13 days beginning on the first Monday of each May, so the same window recurs yearly. The clerk's page adds that postmarks do not count for the appeal form.

  • Bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal, photographs, insurance policies, construction costs, listings or sale contracts.
  • A paid representative must attach a letter of authorization from the owner.
  • Hearings take place at the LFUCG Phoenix Building, 101 East Vine Street, in a first-floor conference room, and the clerk mails each appellant a time.
  • After the roll is finalized, the PVA still accepts a request for review, though it cannot change the bill already issued for that year.

The appeals office at the clerk can be reached at 859-253-3344.

sections.h2: Does Fayette County offer a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Yes. A qualifying home loses $49,100 of assessed value under the exemption, a figure the state set for 2025 and 2026. An owner qualifies by turning 65 at any point in the calendar year or by being classified as totally disabled, and the house must be the primary residence.

The disability route needs total disability status under a public or private retirement system, payments across the calendar year, and a yearly confirmation to the PVA. A copy of the system's disability letter serves as proof. Age can be shown with a driver's license, birth certificate or registration, passport, school record or marriage record.

Each residence gets one exemption and each person gets one. Applications go by mail to the Fayette PVA at 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, by fax to 859-246-2729 or by scan to the PVA's email.

sections.h2: What happens to Fayette County property taxes when I sell my house?
sections.html:
Because the bill is issued to whoever owned the property on January 1, a seller may receive a statement for a year in which the buyer takes title. After a sale, the PVA tries to mail the bill in care of the new owner, though a closing near printing time can outrun the update. Questions about the prorated share go to the closing agent or attorney, because the sheriff does not issue prorated bills or accept prorated payments.

A bill still open after April 15 moves to the County Clerk. The clerk takes only cash, money order or cashier's or certified check payable to the Fayette County Clerk, refuses partial payments and adds interest every month. The County Attorney's Office, at 859-254-4941, handles payment arrangements for owners who cannot pay in full.

Each summer the clerk offers eligible delinquent bills to third-party buyers, somewhere from day 90 to day 135 after the handover. The 2026 sale was July 24. In the Department of Revenue's sample, a $1,000 bill stands at $1,254 on the day it transfers, counting the penalty, the sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission. Clerk and attorney charges come later. A sale ordered by a court, including for delinquent taxes, goes through the Master Commissioner. The clerk also offers a free alert service: register a name or address and an email arrives whenever a document is recorded against it.

sections.h2: How does Fayette County's market look to a seller?
sections.html:
Fayette County is a 286 square mile urban county in the central Bluegrass region, formed by the Virginia General Assembly in 1780 and joined to Lexington as a single government since 1974. Scott, Bourbon, Clark, Madison, Jessamine and Woodford counties surround it, and Lexington is its seat and only city. Census QuickFacts describes a county unlike most in Kentucky:

  • Population: 329,751 in 2025, up 2.2 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Homes: 152,488 housing units, with 53.8 percent owner-occupied.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $293,500, with median gross rent of $1,164.
  • Median household income: $69,479.
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,052.
  • Mean travel time to work: 20.9 minutes.

With nearly half of homes rented and steady permit activity, a house needing repairs or carrying a tax balance still draws buyers. If a sale has to close without repairs or a listing period, a cash buyer who takes the house as-is can pay off the tax from the proceeds.

faqs.q: When is the 2% discount deadline in Fayette County?
faqs.a: The discount ends on November 1 of the assessment year. In 2026 it ran from October 1 to November 1 and cut the bill by 2 percent. After that the bill is due at face value through December 31.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Fayette County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Pay at the Sheriff's Property Tax Division, Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse, 150 North Limestone. The counter takes cash, checks and money orders. Any Lexington Republic Bank lobby also takes payments through January 31 if you bring the bill coupon.

faqs.q: How much is the Fayette County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: For 2026 the deduction is $49,100, taken from the fair cash value of a qualifying primary residence. The owner must be 65 during the calendar year or totally disabled, and the PVA at 859-246-2722 processes applications.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Fayette County assessment after the window closes?
faqs.a: Not for the current bill. The PVA conference and the clerk's appeal filing both fall inside the May inspection period, and the 2026 deadlines were May 18 and May 20. After that you can still request a review through the PVA, but a finalized assessment cannot change the bill for that year.

faqs.q: What if Fayette County taxes stay unpaid?
faqs.a: On April 15 the bill becomes delinquent at 21 percent and passes to the County Clerk, who adds monthly interest and fees. The clerk may then sell the bill to an outside buyer at the summer sale, held on July 24 in 2026.
